summary.title: Out of the Tar Pit
summary.one_liner: Moseley and Marks argue that state, control and code volume are the main accidental sources of software complexity, and propose minimizing them with functional programming and the relational model.
keywords: why is large software hard to understand
testing cannot prove absence of bugs
takeaways: Complexity, especially from mutable state, is the main reason large systems are hard to understand, test and maintain.
Brooks' essential vs accidental complexity distinction is used, but the authors argue most contemporary complexity is accidental.
State makes testing and informal reasoning hard, and stateless code becomes contaminated when it calls stateful code.
Implicit control flow and explicit shared-state concurrency add further complexity that is often unnecessary.
The paper outlines a complexity-minimizing approach combining functional programming ideas with the relational model of data.
summary.summary: The paper opens by arguing that complexity is the root cause of most large-scale software problems, building on Brooks' 'No Silver Bullet' and quotes from Dijkstra, Hoare and others. It identifies state, control (ordering and concurrency) and code volume as the major causes, explaining how each hampers both testing and informal reasoning. It then distinguishes accidental from essential complexity and recommends avoiding causes rather than coping with them. The second half sketches a potential approach based on functional programming and Codd's relational model, with a brief example and comparison to other approaches.
